LC19 · Cardiac & Vascular Microanatomy

LC19 · Endocardium

1A 5-year-old German Shepherd has infective endocarditis with vegetative lesions on the mitral valve leaflets. Damage to this endocardial layer puts the patient at immediate risk for which complication?

  1. Thromboembolism
  2. Pericardial tamponade
  3. Dilated cardiomyopathy
  4. Cardiac ischemia
Tap to reveal answer
Thromboembolism
Endocardial injury disrupts the smooth, non-thrombogenic surface and promotes thrombus formation; valve vegetations can embolize.
LC19 · Tunica adventitia / vasa vasorum

2Immune-mediated vasculitis is concentrated in the tunica adventitia of the thoracic aorta and occludes the vasa vasorum. What is the immediate physiological consequence?

  1. Complete loss of blood flow through the main vessel lumen due to mechanical collapse
  2. Interruption of autonomic neural signaling needed to trigger immediate vasoconstriction
  3. Loss of active transcellular transport systems that pump calcium into the subendothelial matrix
  4. Ischemia and nutrient deprivation localized to the outer layers of the thick vessel wall
Tap to reveal answer
Ischemia and nutrient deprivation localized to the outer layers of the thick vessel wall
Vasa vasorum supply the outer wall of large vessels. Occluding them deprives those outer wall layers of blood and nutrients.
LC19 · Arterioles

3A cat with CKD has severe systemic hypertension. Pathologic narrowing/remodeling of the primary resistance vessels is driving the persistent elevation in pressure. Which arteriolar layer is the principal site of resistance control?

  1. Tunica media elastic lamellae
  2. Tunica adventitia vasa vasorum
  3. Tunica media smooth muscle
  4. Tunica intima internal elastic lamina
Tap to reveal answer
Tunica media smooth muscle
Arterioles regulate resistance through 1–3 layers of smooth muscle in the tunica media.
LC19 · Muscular arteries

4A major systemic vessel has a thick smooth-muscle tunica media with minimal elastic fibers and distinct internal and external elastic laminae. What vessel is this, and what is its primary role?

  1. Muscular artery; distributes blood and regulates organ perfusion
  2. Medium vein; acts as a capacitance vessel holding blood volume
  3. Elastic artery; stores energy during systole to maintain continuous flow
  4. Arteriole; serves as the primary site of total peripheral resistance
Tap to reveal answer
Muscular artery; distributes blood and regulates organ perfusion
Muscular arteries have a prominent smooth-muscle media, few elastic fibers, and distinct elastic laminae; they distribute blood and regulate organ perfusion.
LC19 · Purkinje fibers

5A Boxer has ventricular arrhythmias and subendocardial degeneration. Disruption of which modified cardiac structure is responsible?

  1. Purkinje fibers
  2. Mesothelium
  3. Intercalated discs
  4. Cardiac skeleton
Tap to reveal answer
Purkinje fibers
Purkinje fibers lie in the subendocardial region and rapidly conduct impulses through the ventricles.

LC20 · Electrocardiophysiology

LC20 · HCN / funny current

6A mutation causes the cardiac HCN channel to activate significantly faster during diastole. What is the most likely clinical outcome?

  1. Tachycardia
  2. Ventricular fibrillation
  3. Bradycardia
  4. First-degree atrioventricular block
Tap to reveal answer
Tachycardia
Faster HCN activation steepens phase 4 depolarization so pacemaker cells reach threshold sooner and fire more often.
LC20 · Class III antiarrhythmics

7A patient is treated with amiodarone, a potassium-channel blocker. What is the most likely clinical outcome?

  1. Tachycardia due to accelerated phase 4 spontaneous depolarization in pacemaker nodes.
  2. Bradycardia due to a prolonged cardiac action potential duration and a longer effective refractory period.
  3. Ventricular fibrillation due to enhanced early phase 1 outward potassium currents in the subepicardium.
  4. Premature ventricular contractions due to delayed afterdepolarizations secondary to intracellular calcium overload.
Tap to reveal answer
Bradycardia due to a prolonged cardiac action potential duration and a longer effective refractory period.
Class III K⁺-channel blockade slows repolarization and extends refractoriness.
LC20 · β-blockers

8A canine patient with severe sinus tachycardia is treated with atenolol, a β₁-adrenergic receptor antagonist. What outcome and direct cellular change are expected?

  1. Bradycardia due to activation of inhibitory G-protein subunits by acetylcholine.
  2. Bradycardia due to a decrease in intracellular cyclic AMP (cAMP) levels.
  3. Tachycardia due to increased opening of HCN channels.
  4. Tachycardia due to enhanced calcium influx through Cav1.x channels via PKA.
Tap to reveal answer
Bradycardia due to a decrease in intracellular cyclic AMP (cAMP) levels.
Blocking β₁ signaling lowers cAMP, slows HCN-dependent phase 4 depolarization, and lowers heart rate.
LC20 · Class IV antiarrhythmics

9A patient receives diltiazem, a Class IV antiarrhythmic that blocks slow L-type calcium channels. What is the most likely outcome?

  1. Tachycardia due to a steeper slope of phase 4 spontaneous depolarization in SA nodal cells.
  2. Tachycardia due to a shortened absolute refractory period from accelerated sodium influx.
  3. Bradycardia due to a decreased upstroke velocity during phase 0 depolarization in SA nodal cells.
  4. Bradycardia due to a prolonged phase 3 repolarization duration from delayed potassium efflux.
Tap to reveal answer
Bradycardia due to a decreased upstroke velocity during phase 0 depolarization in SA nodal cells.
SA nodal phase 0 depends on Ca²⁺ entry, so L-type Ca²⁺ blockade slows the nodal upstroke and rate/conduction.
LC20 · Class I / lidocaine

10A dog with severe ventricular tachycardia after GDV surgery is treated with lidocaine, a Class Ib Na⁺-channel blocker. What is the expected outcome?

  1. Resolution of the tachycardia due to a decreased upstroke velocity during phase 0 depolarization in ventricular cardiomyocytes.
  2. Bradycardia due to a decreased slope of phase 4 spontaneous depolarization in SA nodal cells.
  3. Tachycardia due to an increased intracellular calcium transient during phase 2.
  4. Resolution of the tachycardia due to a prolonged phase 2/3 action potential plateau from delayed potassium efflux.
Tap to reveal answer
Resolution of the tachycardia due to a decreased upstroke velocity during phase 0 depolarization in ventricular cardiomyocytes.
Class I drugs block voltage-gated Na⁺ channels used for phase 0 in working ventricular myocardium; SA nodal cells do not depend on these channels.

LC21–22 · ECG Interpretation & Arrhythmias

LC21–22 · P waves / chamber depolarization

11An English Springer Spaniel has severe bradycardia with a regular ventricular escape rhythm and complete absence of P waves. Assuming a primary structural failure of the chambers, which portion of the heart is failing to undergo depolarization?

  1. Atrioventricular (AV) node due to an increased refractory period delaying signal propagation.
  2. Sinoatrial (SA) node due to a lack of intrinsic automaticity to initiate the sinus rhythm.
  3. Ventricular myocardium due to a conduction block at the level of the bundle branches.
  4. Atrial myocardium due to structural or electrical failure preventing the generation of a visible P-wave.
Tap to reveal answer
Atrial myocardium due to structural or electrical failure preventing the generation of a visible P-wave.
Key fix: the question asks which chamber tissue is failing to depolarize. P waves represent atrial depolarization, so complete absence of P waves points to the atrial myocardium.
LC21–22 · ECG voltage

12A Maine Coon with advanced HCM has abnormally tall R waves in Lead II. Based on vector voltage principles, what primarily drives the increased voltage magnitude?

  1. Right-axis deviation due to the electrical vector becoming perpendicular to the measurement lead.
  2. Sinus tachycardia due to increased SA nodal firing.
  3. Pericardial effusion amplifying electrical signal transmission.
  4. Atrial and ventricular myocardial hypertrophy due to increased mass of cardiac tissue undergoing depolarization.
Tap to reveal answer
Atrial and ventricular myocardial hypertrophy due to increased mass of cardiac tissue undergoing depolarization.
Measured voltage magnitude increases with the mass of tissue depolarizing.
LC21–22 · Mean electrical axis

13A dog with severe heartworm disease has right ventricular hypertrophy and pronounced right axis deviation. Which two-lead QRS pattern confirms this?

  1. Positive Lead II and positive Lead I
  2. Negative Lead II and negative Lead I
  3. Positive Lead II and negative Lead I
  4. Negative Lead II and positive Lead I
Tap to reveal answer
Negative Lead II and negative Lead I
Two-lead shortcut: if Lead II is negative, use Lead I; a negative Lead I indicates right axis deviation.
LC21–22 · Rate

14At 50 mm/s, how should this dog's cardiac rate be classified?

  1. Normal rate
  2. Bradycardia
  3. Not enough information
  4. Tachycardia
Tap to reveal answer
Tachycardia
The tracing displays a heart rate around 166 bpm, and the lecture example labels ~165 bpm in a dog as slightly tachycardic.
LC21–22 · Rhythm

15Across the entire strip, how should the R–R rhythm be classified?

  1. Regular (Rhythmic)
  2. Regularly irregular (Arrhythmic with a pattern)
  3. Irregularly irregular (Arrhythmic without a pattern)
  4. Paroxysmal episodic (Arrhythmic in bursts)
Tap to reveal answer
Regular (Rhythmic)
Key fix: the R–R intervals are consistent enough to classify this strip as regular/rhythmic.
LC21–22 · P and QRS

16Which statement best describes the P-wave/QRS relationship on this strip?

  1. There are QRS complexes without preceding P waves; ventricles are depolarizing on their own.
  2. There is a P wave for every QRS complex and a QRS complex for every P wave; the SA node is in control.
  3. There are P waves not followed by QRS complexes; the AV node is failing to conduct.
  4. There is a 1:1 P-to-QRS ratio, but broad complexes imply ventricular automaticity bypassed the SA node.
Tap to reveal answer
There is a P wave for every QRS complex and a QRS complex for every P wave; the SA node is in control.
The tracing shows a consistent 1:1 P-to-QRS relationship.
LC21–22 · Atrial fibrillation

17An Irish Wolfhound has a rapid, irregularly irregular rhythm and the ECG strip shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?

  1. Atrial fibrillation due to chaotic atrial electrical activity with no P waves and irregularly irregular ventricular response.
  2. Ventricular tachycardia due to a ventricular ectopic focus with a regular rhythm and wide bizarre QRS complexes.
  3. Atrial standstill with bradycardia and a regular junctional escape rhythm.
  4. Sinus tachycardia due to accelerated SA-node phase 4 depolarization creating a rapid but regular rhythm.
Tap to reveal answer
Atrial fibrillation due to chaotic atrial electrical activity with no P waves and irregularly irregular ventricular response.
No distinct P waves plus an irregularly irregular R–R pattern is the classic lecture pattern for atrial fibrillation.
LC21–22 · AV blocks

18Which diagnosis best fits this Lead II rhythm strip?

  1. First-degree AV block
  2. Second-degree AV block
  3. Third-degree (complete) AV block
  4. Sick sinus syndrome
Tap to reveal answer
Second-degree AV block
Key fix: atrial activity continues, but at least one atrial impulse is not followed by a QRS complex — an intermittently dropped ventricular response.
LC21–22 · Ventricular tachycardia

19A telemetry strip abruptly transitions from a normal sinus beat into a rapid sustained run of abnormal waveforms. What is the most accurate diagnosis?

  1. Atrial premature contractions
  2. Ventricular tachycardia
  3. Supraventricular tachycardia
  4. Atrial fibrillation
Tap to reveal answer
Ventricular tachycardia
The run consists of rapid, repetitive abnormal ventricular complexes, matching the lecture's ventricular tachycardia pattern.
LC21–22 · Pacemakers

20A dog has symptomatic third-degree AV block that fails medical therapy. What is the most appropriate long-term management?

  1. Chronic oral pimobendan therapy
  2. Continuous IV lidocaine CRI
  3. Left auricular surgical appendage ligation
  4. Pacemaker implantation
Tap to reveal answer
Pacemaker implantation
Pacemakers maintain heart rate when intrinsic pacing/conduction is inadequate and are indicated for advanced AV block.
LC21–22 · Defibrillation

21A collapsed dog has ventricular fibrillation with no identifiable QRS complexes or pulses. What electrical intervention should be performed immediately?

  1. Pacemaker implantation
  2. Defibrillation
  3. Cardioversion
Tap to reveal answer
Defibrillation
Ventricular fibrillation is treated with an immediate unsynchronized defibrillation shock.
LC21–22 · Ventricular tachycardia treatment

22A dog develops sustained ventricular tachycardia after GDV surgery. Which antiarrhythmic drug is the most appropriate first-line medical therapy?

  1. Atropine
  2. Lidocaine
  3. Digoxin
  4. Diltiazem
Tap to reveal answer
Lidocaine
The lecture identifies lidocaine as the emergency antiarrhythmic for ventricular tachyarrhythmias.

Muscle spindle

Smooth muscle, longitudinal section

LC19 · Purkinje fibers

25Identify the pale, fluid-filled fibers in the endocardial region.

Tap to reveal answer
Purkinje fibers
They are large, pale modified cardiac myocytes in the subendocardial region with fewer myofibrils and more glycogen.
LC19 · Epicardium

26Identify the connective tissue layer on the outer surface of the heart.

Tap to reveal answer
Epicardium
The outer heart layer consists of mesothelium plus underlying connective tissue/adipose and is continuous with the visceral pericardium.
LC19 · Muscular artery

27Identify the vessel type in this histology image.

  1. Elastic artery
  2. Vein
  3. Arteriole
  4. Capillary
  5. Venule
  6. Lymphatic vessel
  7. Muscular artery
Tap to reveal answer
Muscular artery
The vessel has a thick smooth-muscle tunica media and a relatively small, maintained lumen without the multiple elastic lamellae of an elastic artery.

Bone Physiology

Bone physiology · outside uploaded cardiovascular lecture set

28Which bone-matrix component primarily gives bone its compressive strength and hardness?

  1. Matrix metalloproteases
  2. Osteocalcin
  3. Type I collagen
  4. Hydroxyapatite mineral deposits
Tap to reveal answer
Hydroxyapatite mineral deposits
Hydroxyapatite provides mineral hardness and compressive strength; this point is not in the uploaded cardiovascular lectures.
Bone physiology · outside uploaded cardiovascular lecture set

29A pharmaceutical inhibits sclerostin activity. What change in bone tissue is expected?

  1. Decreased bone density due to increased osteoclast activity
  2. Increased bone density due to decreased osteocyte activity
  3. Decreased bone density due to decreased osteoblast activity
  4. Increased bone density due to increased osteoblast activity
Tap to reveal answer
Increased bone density due to increased osteoblast activity
Sclerostin normally inhibits bone formation; blocking it increases osteoblast-driven bone formation. Not covered in the uploaded cardiovascular lectures.
Bone physiology · outside uploaded cardiovascular lecture set

30After weeks of immobilization for a tibial fracture, why should return to normal load bearing be gradual?

  1. Type I collagen is only produced when the limb is completely unloaded.
  2. Bone under load permanently stops remodeling.
  3. Osteoclasts are inactive during all fracture healing.
  4. Underloaded bone becomes weaker and needs mechanical stress to remodel appropriately.
Tap to reveal answer
Underloaded bone becomes weaker and needs mechanical stress to remodel appropriately.
Bone adapts to mechanical loading; prolonged underloading weakens it, so reloading should be progressive. Not covered in the uploaded cardiovascular lectures.
Ultra-fast anchors: Endocardium damage → thrombus · vasa vasorum feed outer vessel wall · arteriolar media controls resistance · Purkinje = pale subendocardial conduction cells · HCN faster = faster HR · Class III blocks K⁺ · β-blockers ↓cAMP · Class IV slows nodal Ca²⁺ phase 0 · lidocaine blocks ventricular Na⁺ phase 0 · P wave = atrial depolarization · both Lead I & II negative = right axis · Q14 tachycardia · Q15 regular · Q17 AFib · Q18 2° AV block · Q19 V-tach · 3° AV block → pacemaker · V-fib → defibrillate · V-tach → lidocaine.
